question: In Albania, there is currently a popular movement opposing tourism development projects on Sazan Island and within the Vjosa-Narta protected area financed by Jared Kushner’s investment fund. These demonstrations reflect the view that Albania should not be sold off piecemeal for the benefit of the private interests of the ultra-rich and the imperial ambitions associated with the Trump family.

These hotel developments pose risks to protected coastal and marine ecosystems and biodiversity, as well as to the habitats of threatened species. Sazan Island is located within the Karaburun-Sazan Marine National Park, which is designated as a Specially Protected Area of Mediterranean Importance (SPAMI).

These projects therefore raise questions regarding their compatibility with Albania’s commitments under its EU accession process, particularly with regard to alignment with the EU environmental acquis. 1.

How does the Commission assess the compatibility of real estate investments linked to the family of a non-EU head of state with the standards of transparency and good governance expected from countries seeking accession to the EU?

Given the concerns already expressed by the EU regarding the 2024 amendments to Albania’s law on protected areas, what measures does the Commission intend to take to ensure that these mega-projects do not undermine Albania’s alignment with the EU environmental acquis?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.8.2026) The Commission is closely following Albania’s progress in aligning with the EU acquis. Foreign investments can bring benefits, provided they are transparent and in line with national and EU rules. Developments in the area of environment and nature protection are assessed in the context of Albania’s accession negotiations.

Under Chapter 27 – Environment and climate change, Albania has to align its legislation with the EU environmental acquis, including the Environmental Impact Assessment1 and the Strategic Environmental Assessment2 Directives, and the Birds3 and Habitats4 Directives.

Furthermore, the closing benchmarks explicitly require Albania to align with the EU nature protection acquis, including by repealing incompatible provisions introduced through amendments to the law on Protected Areas and terminating the 2015 legislation on strategic investments.

They also require Albania to demonstrate adequate capacity to manage future Natura 2000 sites and to ensure effective conservation measures preventing habitat and species deterioration. The Commission is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society regarding the project in the Pishë Poro - Nartë area.

This project, like all ongoing projects in Albania, will need to comply with the benchmarks set under Chapter 27. The Commission has encouraged the Albanian authorities to continue taking steps supporting the fulfilment of the closing benchmarks and move forward on its EU path and it will monitor closely such fulfilment.
The Government of Albania is assuring that a full environmental impact assessment will be carried out and that European environmental standards will be respected.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment

of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, pp. 1–21. 2 Directive 2001/42/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 June 2001 on the assessment of the effects of certain plans and programmes on the environment, OJ L 197, 21.7.2001, pp. 30–37.

3 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, pp. 7–25. 4 Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, pp. 7–50.
